questions.prompt: It's 10:45 AM on a Tuesday and you still have 4 untouched leads sitting in your NEW LEAD bucket. What should you do in the next 15 minutes?
choices: Dial and text all 4 before 11 AM so the NEW LEAD section is empty — speed-to-lead on fresh leads is the single highest-leverage action you can take.
Text all 4 now and dial them this afternoon once your current cadence is done.
Leave them — you'll get to them after your morning power-dial block.
Ask your pod leader to reassign them since you're clearly overloaded.
questions.explanation: The 11 AM rule says New Leads must be empty by 11 AM — one dial and one text, minimum, on each. Texting only or deferring defeats the point, which is to force the right behavior: speed-to-lead on fresh leads is your single highest-leverage action.

questions.prompt: A rookie rep finishes week one with 6 sales and tells you she's worried she's in the wrong job. What's the most accurate response?
choices: She should probably talk to HR about exiting before week two.
She's behind — average rookies hit 25 in week one.
She needs to shorten her lunch breaks to catch up.

Week one is realistically 7–11 sales and the first calls are awkward by design — don't let week-one discomfort convince her she's in the wrong job. Ramp climbs through weeks 6–8 when 25+ becomes routine.
questions.explanation: The ramp expectation for week 1 is explicitly 7–11 sales, and the module calls out that week-one discomfort is not a signal to quit. 25+/week doesn't become routine until weeks 6–8 — pushing her to skip lunch contradicts the culture rule on breaks.

questions.prompt: You live-dial a Pacific-time lead and get no answer at 4:30 PM your time. You're on Eastern. What's the correct next action?
choices: Leave a manual voicemail explaining who you are and what you do.
Keep redialing every 10 minutes until they pick up.
Hang up with no voicemail — manual VMs tank callback rates; batch the no-answer into an end-of-day VM drop instead.
Text them 'Is now a good time?' to confirm availability.
questions.explanation: The rule is to never leave a voicemail manually — missed calls without VMs get returned more often than those with them. VM drops are batched end-of-day via automation. Redialing repeatedly burns the lead, and 'is now a good time?' is a banned phrase.

questions.prompt: You end the day with 3 unread SMS in your inbox because they came in while you were on a long call. What's the expectation?
choices: Clear all 3 before logging off — zero unread at end of day, no exceptions.
Leave them for tomorrow — fresh eyes are better.
Mark them read and move on without responding.
Reply only if they look high-intent.
questions.explanation: The text rule is explicit: zero unread at end of day, no exceptions, and be the last person to send. Even a 'no thanks' gets a polite closing text so you own the last word. Marking unread without replying violates both rules.

questions.prompt: You just finished a rough call where a lead hung up on you mid-pitch. What should you do in the next 60 seconds?
choices: Go take a 20-minute walk to shake it off.
Vent in the team chat about the lead being rude.
Relisten to the call immediately before making another dial.
Ask yourself what question you missed and what you learned, then get back on the phone inside 60 seconds.
questions.explanation: The post-rough-call self-talk is 'what question did I miss, what did I learn?' — then back on the phone inside 60 seconds. Walks are for between dial blocks, not after every bad call. Venting and immediate self-review stall momentum.

questions.prompt: It's Saturday at 8:15 AM and you want to power through your West Coast list. Why is this a violation of the weekend rules?
choices: Weekend calling is banned entirely.
You should only call East Coast on weekends.
Earliest weekend call is 9 AM local time, with 10 AM as the sweet spot — 8:15 AM local is too early and will hurt your brand.
Weekends require a pod leader's written approval.
questions.explanation: Weekend calling is optional and capped at 2–3 hours, with 9 AM local as the earliest and 10 AM as the sweet spot. Calling at 8:15 AM local violates the time-zone rule and makes you the person the lead didn't want a call from.

questions.prompt: A rep is rolling into week 4 and tells you she still feels nervous on every call and is reading from her notes. Which part of the confidence curve is this, and what's the honest read?
choices: She's in the normal 'five clicks less nervous' weeks 3–4 zone — knows the pitch but still in her head. Weeks 5–6 are when she'll start asking real questions and disagreeing with leads.
She's broken — by week 4 reps should be fully automatic.
She should be a pod leader candidate already.
She needs to restart the training from module 1.
questions.explanation: Weeks 3–4 are explicitly the 'five clicks less nervous, knows the pitch, still in her head' phase of the confidence curve. The pitch doesn't become automatic until week 8+. Her ramp is on track, not broken.

questions.prompt: Your weekly call-review habit requires you to pull three of your own calls. Which mix teaches you the most?
choices: Three wins so you can replicate what worked.
Three losses so you know exactly what to fix.
One win and two losses — losses reveal gaps, and the one win anchors what already works.
Three random calls chosen by your pod leader.
questions.explanation: The self-review spec is explicitly one win and two losses per week. Losses are where the improvement lives; the single win anchors what's working. All-wins teaches nothing new; all-losses erodes confidence.

questions.prompt: A lead tells you your Tier 2 pricing sounds high. You start the response with 'I totally understand...' Why is this a problem on a performance-standards basis?
choices: 'I totally understand' is a banned phrase — it sounds trained, and it violates the voice expectation. A sincere one-word ack like 'Gotcha' plus a question performs measurably better.
It's too long to say on the phone.
It's grammatically incorrect.
Leads don't like the word 'totally.'
questions.explanation: 'I totally understand' is on the banned-phrase list because it signals script-delivery and puts the lead on guard. Replace with a single sincere word then a question. The rule isn't stylistic — it's measured against actual close rates.

questions.prompt: Your rolling four-week average is 22 memberships a week: 30, 14, 26, 18. Your manager asks if you're on track. What's the most honest answer?
choices: No — week two was 14 and that's a failure.
No — every week must be 25 or higher.
Yes — any average above 10 is acceptable.
Yes — the target is 25/week but what matters is the rolling four-week average; 22 is close and some weeks you'll hit 30 and some 14, and both are normal.
questions.explanation: The target is 25/week measured on a rolling four-week average. The module explicitly says some weeks you'll hit 30, some 14, and both are normal. 22 is slightly under target but within the expected variance — not a failure and not weekly pass/fail.
